transcription.tex: A \textbf{matrix} (plural: matrices) is an array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.\[\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-2\\3&3&0\end{pmatrix}\]
A matrix organises several values into one structure.

\textbf{Why use matrices?}\par They represent linear transformations, including rotations, reflections and enlargements, and help solve simultaneous equations.\par In 3D graphics, matrices control transformations and camera angles.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: In computer science, matrices are also called arrays. This example records the top five teams in a Premier League table.\par Columns: matches played, won, drawn, lost, goals for, goals against, goal difference, points.
There are \textbf{5 rows} and \textbf{8 columns}: a \(5\times8\) matrix.

transcription.tex: The dimension of a matrix is its number of rows followed by its number of columns.

transcription.tex: Matrices may use square or curved brackets. A matrix with one column is a column vector; a matrix with one row is a row vector.
Matrix variables use \textbf{bold capital letters}; vector variables use bold lowercase letters.

Dimensions are usually clear from the context. Identity matrices are particularly useful in multiplication.

slides.title: Proof for the Formula of the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix

transcription.tex: For interest: derive the inverse by row operations. Let \(\Delta=ad-bc\ne0\). For \(a\ne0\), start with\[\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}a&b&1&0\\c&d&0&1\end{array}\right]\]Divide row 1 by \(a\), then subtract \(c\) times row 1 from row 2:\[\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1&b/a&1/a&0\\0&\Delta/a&-c/a&1\end{array}\right]\]

Multiply row 2 by \(a/\Delta\), then subtract \(b/a\) times row 2 from row 1:\[\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1&0&d/\Delta&-b/\Delta\\0&1&-c/\Delta&a/\Delta\end{array}\right]\]\[M^{-1}=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\]If \(a=0\), interchange the rows first. The same formula also follows by multiplying the proposed inverse by \(M\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: The transpose \(A^T\) interchanges rows and columns.\[\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\2&5\\3&6\end{pmatrix}\]An \(m\times n\) matrix becomes \(n\times m\).

Beyond the exam: transposition moves a transformation between the two vectors in a dot product.\[(A\mathbf u)\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf u\cdot(A^T\mathbf v)\]\[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}5\\6\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}7\\8\end{pmatrix}\]\[\begin{pmatrix}17\\39\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}7\\8\end{pmatrix}=431\]\[\begin{pmatrix}5\\6\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}31\\46\end{pmatrix}=431\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{5. Coincident planes}\par If all three equations describe the same plane, every point on that plane is a solution.\[x+2y-z=3\]\[2x+4y-2z=6\]\[-x-2y+z=-3\]

All three equations are multiples of one another.\par The system is consistent with infinitely many solutions.\par A zero determinant alone does not tell us whether there are no solutions or infinitely many: we must inspect the equations.

transcription.tex: 5. These planes do not intersect at a single point. Find \(a\) and describe their intersection.\[\begin{aligned}x+ay+2z&=a\\x-y-z&=a\\x+4y+4z&=0\end{aligned}\]
